passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: Why the sky is blue. Sunlight holds every colour, and the air bounces the blue part all over the sky.

passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: Look up on a clear day and the sky is blue. Yet the light that fills it comes from the Sun, and sunlight is white. White light is every colour mixed together. A rainbow shows this, because it pulls the colours apart.

passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: Light moves in waves. Each colour has its own wavelength, the gap from the top of one wave to the top of the next. Blue light has short waves, about 450 nanometres long. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Red light has longer waves, about 700 nanometres.

passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: Air is made of tiny bits called molecules, far smaller than a wave of light. When light hits one, some of it bounces off in a new direction. This is called scattering. Short waves scatter much more than long ones. Make a wave half as long and it scatters sixteen times as much.

passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: So blue light scatters about 5.9 times as much as red. As sunlight crosses the air, blue light is thrown all over the sky. Wherever you look, some of that blue reaches your eyes. Red and yellow light mostly go straight on.

passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: Violet waves are shorter still, so why is the sky not violet? The Sun sends out less violet light than blue, and our eyes are less able to see it. Blue wins.

passages.title: Why the sky is blue
passages.text: At sunset the Sun is low. Its light must cross much more air to reach you. On the way, most of the blue is scattered off to the side. What is left is the orange and red light that paints the evening sky.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: Why February gets a 29th. The Earth takes a little more than 365 days to go round the Sun, and an extra day every four years keeps the calendar in step.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: A year is the time the Earth takes to go once round the Sun, from one spring to the next. That takes about 365.2422 days. It is not a whole number of days, and that small extra bit causes all the trouble.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: A normal calendar year has 365 days. So each year the calendar ends a bit too soon, by 0.2422 of a day. That is nearly six hours. After four years the calendar is almost a whole day behind the Sun.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: The fix is to add one day every fourth year, on February 29. A year with this extra day is called a leap year. It pulls the calendar back in line with the seasons.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: But the true gap is a little less than a quarter of a day. Adding a whole day every four years is slightly too much, and over time the calendar would run ahead.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: So there is a second rule. A year that divides by 4 is a leap year. A year that divides by 100 is not, unless it also divides by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.

passages.title: Why February gets a 29th
passages.text: That gives 97 leap days in every 400 years. The average calendar year comes out at 365.2425 days, very close to the real one. Without leap days, the seasons would slide by about 24 days every hundred years. In time, July would come in the middle of winter for people in the north.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: How your phone knows where it is. Your phone listens to clocks in space and turns how late their signals arrive into distances.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: Open a map on your phone and a dot shows where you stand. The phone works this out by listening to satellites. It does not send anything back to them. It only listens.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: There are about 31 working GPS satellites. They circle the Earth about 20,200 kilometres up, twice a day. Each one carries a very exact clock. Over and over, each one sends out a signal that says which satellite it is and what time it is.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, but even light takes time to cross that gap. The phone notes how late each signal arrives. The delay tells it how far away that satellite is.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: One distance is not enough. It only says you are somewhere on a huge circle around that satellite. Add a second satellite and the two circles cross at two points. A third circle picks out just one of them. That point is you.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: Then why does a phone need 4 satellites? The clock inside a phone is cheap and a little off. Because light is so fast, a tiny clock error turns into a big error in distance. The fourth signal lets the phone fix its own clock while it works out where it is.

passages.title: How your phone knows where it is
passages.text: Out in the open, a phone is usually right to within about 5 metres. Tall buildings and trees block and bounce the signals, so in a city the dot can wander.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: What a gigabyte holds. Each step from kilobyte to terabyte is a thousand times bigger, and everyday things sit on every rung.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: Everything a computer stores is made of bits. A bit is a tiny switch that is either on or off. Put 8 bits together and you have a byte. One byte can hold one letter, like a single A.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: Bytes add up fast, so we use bigger units. Each step up is a thousand times the one before. A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes. A megabyte is 1,000 kilobytes. A gigabyte is 1,000 megabytes, and a terabyte is 1,000 gigabytes.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: Real things help to picture this ladder. A page of plain text has about 2,000 letters, so it fills about 2 kilobytes. A whole book of 500 pages fits in about 1 megabyte. A film on a DVD takes about 4.7 gigabytes. A 1 terabyte drive could hold about 200 of those films.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: There is a catch. Computers count in twos, not tens. So to a computer, a kilobyte is often 1,024 bytes, not 1,000. At each step up the ladder, the gap grows. A drive sold as 1 terabyte shows up on a computer as about 931 gigabytes. No space has gone missing.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: The shop and the computer are just using different units.

passages.title: What a gigabyte holds
passages.text: Next time your phone says it is full, think of the ladder. A few films take far more room than thousands of pages of notes. Photos and videos are what fill a phone, not words.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: Why ice floats. Water grows when it freezes, so ice is lighter than the water around it and lakes freeze from the top down.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: Drop an ice cube into a glass of water and it bobs at the top. That seems normal, but it is odd. Most liquids shrink when they freeze, and the solid sinks. Water does the opposite.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: Water is made of tiny bits called molecules that tug on each other. In liquid water they tumble about and crowd close together. When water freezes, they lock into a neat pattern of six-sided rings, like a honeycomb. Each ring has open space in the middle.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: Because of those gaps, water grows by about 9 percent when it freezes. That is why a full bottle of water can crack in the freezer. The same water now needs more room.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: A thing floats when it is lighter than the same amount of the liquid around it. A litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram. A litre of ice weighs only about 0.917 kilograms. So ice floats, with a small part of it poking above the surface.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: This matters for life. Water is heaviest at about 4 °C. In winter, a lake cools from the top. Once the top water is colder than 4 °C, it gets lighter and stays on top. There it freezes into a lid of ice. Under the lid, the water at the bottom stays near 4 °C.

passages.title: Why ice floats
passages.text: Fish can live through the winter down there.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: How tides work. The Moon pulls the oceans into two bulges, and the Earth turns through both of them every day.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: Spend a day at the seaside and you will see the water creep up the beach and slide back again. These slow rises and falls are the tides. They are caused mostly by the Moon.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: The Moon's gravity pulls on the whole Earth. But it pulls hardest on the side nearest to it and least on the far side. The ocean facing the Moon is pulled toward it and heaps up into a bulge.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: On the far side, the ocean is pulled least of all. It gets left behind a little, so a second bulge forms there too. That is why there are two bulges, one on each side of the Earth.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: The Earth spins through both bulges. Each time your beach passes under one, you get a high tide. The Moon is also moving along its path, so a full turn back to the Moon takes about 24 hours and 50 minutes. Most coasts get two high tides in that time, and they come a little later each day.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: The Sun makes tides too, but it is so far away that its effect is smaller. The Moon's pull on the tides is about 2.2 times the Sun's. At new Moon and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls add together. The tides are bigger, and these are called spring tides.

passages.title: How tides work
passages.text: At half Moon, the two pull at right angles. The tides are smaller, and these are called neap tides.
